The document outlines the different types of tenancies in the public sector, focusing on Assured Periodic Tenancies (APT), Excluded Tenancies or Licenses, and Regulated Tenancies. An APT applies when the property is the tenant's main accommodation, the tenant has their own room, and the landlord does not live there. Excluded tenancies or licenses may occur when the landlord and tenant share living spaces. Regulated tenancies, starting before 15 January 1989, provide tenants with increased protection from eviction and the option to apply for a 'fair rent'. Landlords are responsible for renting out their properties.

Workers in the UK are entitled to 5.6 weeks (28 days for a 5-day work week) of paid annual leave, which includes agency workers, those with irregular hours, and part-year workers. Part-time workers receive the same entitlement, but it will be fewer than 28 days if they work less than 5 days a week. For workers with irregular hours or who work part of the year, leave is accrued based on the hours already worked. However, for leave years beginning before April 2024, the entitlement can be estimated based on the average days or hours worked per week. Employers can include bank holidays as part of statutory annual leave.

The flu vaccine is recommended annually for individuals at higher risk of severe flu complications, including the elderly, those with long-term health conditions, pregnant women, care home residents, primary caregivers, and frontline health and social care workers. Eligible individuals can receive the free NHS flu vaccine, which is offered for conditions such as asthma, heart conditions, chronic kidney disease, liver disease, neurological disorders, diabetes, weakened immune systems, and certain weight issues. To confirm eligibility, individuals should consult their GP surgery or specialist. The NHS will notify eligible individuals when they can receive the vaccine, which can be obtained from their GP surgery or pharmacy.

Norovirus can occur at any time of the year, not just winter. Self-treatment at home is usually sufficient, with rest, plenty of fluids, and over-the-counter medications like paracetamol recommended. Avoiding fruit juice, fizzy drinks, and giving children under 12 medications to stop diarrhea is advised. A pharmacist can be consulted for severe cases, dehydration, or if additional medication is needed to stop diarrhea.

The document outlines symptoms of sepsis in babies, children, and adults. In babies and children, symptoms include difficulty breathing, fits, temperature changes, skin color changes, a non-fading rash, changes in feeding habits, and reduced urination. For children under 5, not being interested in feeding or frequent vomiting may also be signs. A video is provided to help identify symptoms in young children. In adults, symptoms include confusion, uncontrollable shivering, muscle pain, difficulty breathing, skin color changes, temperature changes, and reduced urination. Sepsis symptoms can be harder to notice in certain groups such as babies, young children, people with dementia, learning disabilities, or communication difficulties.

Asthma is characterized by breathing problems such as wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and a tight chest. Symptoms can be mild or severe, and they often worsen at night and early morning. An asthma attack is a severe episode that makes breathing difficult and can be life-threatening. Triggers can include exercise, air pollution, cold air, and allergens like pollen, dust, mould, or animals. Asthma typically starts in children but can occur at any age.

For non-urgent cases, seek advice from a GP if asthma symptoms persist, treatments are ineffective, or the patient needs help with inhaler usage or if symptoms are affecting daily activities or sleep.

High blood pressure is common, particularly in older adults, often showing no symptoms. Risk factors include age, family history, ethnicity, unhealthy diet, being overweight, smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, and prolonged stress. It's recommended to get a blood pressure check at a pharmacy or GP surgery if one is over 40 and hasn't had a check in over 5 years, or if one suspects high blood pressure. Some pharmacies offer free checks for over 40s. Symptoms of high blood pressure are usually absent, but can include headaches, blurred vision, and chest pain. If experiencing frequent headaches, blurred vision, or chest pain, seek urgent help from NHS 111.

If food poisoning occurs, symptoms typically improve within a week. Home treatment includes rest, plenty of fluids, and avoiding spicy or fatty foods. Paracetamol can be used for discomfort, but aspirin and medicines to stop diarrhea are not recommended for children under 12. A pharmacist can provide advice on managing dehydration, oral rehydration solutions, and medicines to stop diarrhea for a short period. In urgent cases, call 111 for advice if a baby under 12 months is affected, a child stops feeding, or a child under 5 shows signs of dehydration.
